passage:
Monday. At playgroup, Shreya, five, grabbed the doll out of Nazia's hands. When Nazia reached for it, Shreya shouted, "Nazia is being MEAN! She's so angry!" Her own fists were clenched tight.
Wednesday. The same thing happened with the swing. "You're angry at me!" Shreya yelled, stamping.
The teacher knelt. "Your fists look tight. Are you feeling angry?"
Shreya stamped again. "No! SHE is!"
Friday. Shreya snatched a crayon, then stopped. She looked down at her fist. "I'm... cross," she mumbled, and gave the crayon back.

qa.q: What did Shreya grab from Nazia on Monday?
qa.a: The doll.

qa.q: Why does Shreya shout that Nazia is angry?
qa.a: Being the grabby, angry one feels bad to own, so it's easier for Shreya to see the anger in Nazia instead of in herself.

qa.q: What did the teacher's question on Wednesday set up for Friday?
qa.a: Pointing out Shreya's tight fists gave her words for her own anger, so by Friday she could spot it herself and give the crayon back.

qa.q: What is it like for Nazia to be called mean after losing the doll?
qa.a: Nazia probably feels confused and unfairly blamed, since Shreya took the doll and then called her the angry one 😢

grounding: Over a week, a five-year-old who snatches toys and calls the other child angry slowly learns to name her own anger.

passage:
Rain had cancelled the park, so Hafsa from downstairs came up to Nitin's small flat, where only one toy car still had working batteries. After Hafsa had driven it for a while, Nitin, five, grabbed the remote.
"Hafsa is mean!" he yelled, red in the face. "She's angry at me! Look at her angry face!"
Hafsa wasn't angry. She was crying.
His Amma, with the pressure cooker whistling, turned off the flame and came over. "Your face is red and your voice is loud," she said. "I think somebody is angry, and that's okay. What can we do with the car?"
Nitin looked at the remote. "Take turns?"

qa.q: How many toy cars still had working batteries?
qa.a: Only one.

qa.q: Why does Nitin insist Hafsa has an angry face?
qa.a: Grabbing the remote left Nitin angry and uneasy, and pinning the anger on Hafsa feels easier than owning it himself 😠

qa.q: What choice did Amma make despite the whistling cooker?
qa.a: She turned off the flame, calmly described Nitin's red face and loud voice and said anger is okay, which helped him think of taking turns.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel being called angry while she's crying?
qa.a: Hafsa likely feels hurt and misunderstood, since she's sad about losing the car, not angry.

grounding: On a rainy day in a small flat, a five-year-old grabs a shared toy and calls the other child angry until his mother names his own feeling.

passage:
In the park of their Delhi colony, Imran was filling a red bucket with sand when Usha, five, yanked it away. Sand sprayed all over his shoes.
"Imran is so angry!" Usha announced to the whole sandpit, pointing. "He's being mean to me!"
Imran just blinked, sandy and silent.
Usha's Nani, knitting on the bench, came and sat at the edge of the sandpit. "Imran looks surprised to me. Show me your own face." She held up her little mirror. Usha saw her scrunched eyebrows and let go of the bucket.
"Maybe I'm the cross one," she said in a small voice.

qa.q: What colour was the bucket?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why does Usha tell the whole sandpit that Imran is angry?
qa.a: Owning her own grabbing and anger feels bad, so it seems more bearable to Usha to put the anger on Imran.

qa.q: What choice of Nani's helped Usha see her own feeling?
qa.a: Nani gently said Imran looked surprised and held up a mirror, so Usha could notice her own scrunched face without being scolded.

qa.q: How might Imran see being called mean after losing his bucket?
qa.a: Imran is probably confused, since he was playing quietly and ended up sandy and blamed.

grounding: A five-year-old snatches a bucket and declares the other child angry until her grandmother helps her see her own cross face.

passage: "Mummy! Pallavi is being MEAN! She's so angry at me!" "Pallavi, are you angry?" "No, I'm sad. Uday took my crayons." "I'm just holding them!" "Uday, whose crayons are in your hand?" "...Hers. But she's angry." "Your face looks very cross, beta. Your fists are tight. Mine get tight when I'm angry too." Uday looked down at his fists. Then, very slowly, he held out two crayons. "Only the red and blue." Pallavi sniffed. "Thank you." Uday stamped off to the sofa, still frowning.

qa.q: What did Uday hold out to Pallavi?
qa.a: Only the red and blue crayons.

qa.q: Why did Uday keep saying Pallavi was the angry one?
qa.a: He had grabbed the crayons and felt angry himself, but owning that felt too bad, so he pushed the angry feeling onto her.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Uday notice his own feeling?
qa.a: She pointed out his cross face and tight fists and said her own fists get tight when she's angry, without shaming him.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel being called mean and angry when she felt sad?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel confused and hurt, since her crayons were taken and then she was blamed for being angry.

grounding: A young boy who took Pallavi's crayons shouts that she is mean and angry, placing his own anger outside himself.

passage: Kindergarten note, Thursday. At block play, Ira (5) pulled a truck from Tashi, then shouted, "Tashi is mean! Tashi is angry at me!" Tashi just sat there, surprised. Ira's own face was red, her hands clenched on the truck. I knelt and said, "I see a very angry face. Whose anger is it?" "Tashi's!" I didn't argue. "When I grab things, my tummy feels hot and angry. Is yours hot?" A tiny nod. We took three slow breaths, and she gave the truck back. I'll tell her mother at pickup today. — Pema

qa.q: What did Ira pull away from Tashi?
qa.a: A truck.

qa.q: Why did Ira shout that Tashi was angry when Tashi just sat there?
qa.a: Ira was the angry one after grabbing the truck, and admitting it felt too bad, so she saw the anger in Tashi instead.

qa.q: Which of Pema's steps helped Ira own the feeling?
qa.a: Not arguing, describing Pema's own hot, angry tummy, asking Ira gently, then breathing together.

qa.q: How might Tashi have felt being shouted at across the room?
qa.a: Tashi looked surprised and was probably confused and a little upset, having done nothing wrong.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young girl who grabbed a toy accusing the other child of anger, placing her own anger outside.

passage: At the Mysuru preschool, Nandini grabbed the red truck from Imran's hands. Imran reached for it. Nandini hid it behind her back and shouted, "Imran is being mean! He's angry at me!" Imran's eyes filled with tears. He wasn't angry; he was sad. The teacher came over. "Nandini, who has the truck?" Nandini's cheeks were red and her fists were tight. "Me. But he's angry." The teacher knelt. "I think maybe someone feels cross. Is it you?" Nandini looked at her fists. "A little." "Thank you for telling me. Let's give it back and find you a truck too."

qa.q: What did Nandini grab from Imran?
qa.a: The red truck.

qa.q: Why did Nandini say Imran was angry when she had grabbed the truck?
qa.a: Nandini was the one feeling cross, but owning that felt too bad, so she put the angry feeling on Imran.

qa.q: What helped Nandini admit her feeling?
qa.a: The teacher gently asked if maybe she felt cross, without scolding, which made it safe for her to say "a little".

qa.q: How might Imran feel being called angry?
qa.a: Imran probably feels confused and sad, since he wasn't angry, just upset that his truck was taken.

grounding: Shows a young child who snatched a toy shouting that the other child is angry and mean, placing her own anger outside herself.

passage:
Monday: Bhavna snatched Ujjwal's crayons and scribbled on his drawing. Ujjwal yelled. "Mummy! Ujjwal is angry at me!" Bhavna cried. Mummy saw the crayons in Bhavna's fist.
Wednesday: At bedtime Mummy read a story about a cross bear who said the rabbit was cross. "Who was really cross?" Mummy asked. Bhavna giggled. "The bear!"
Friday: Bhavna grabbed Ujjwal's ball, then stopped. She looked at her hand. "Mummy, I'm cross because I want the ball." Mummy hugged her and they asked Ujjwal for a turn.

qa.q: What did Mummy read at bedtime on Wednesday?
qa.a: A story about a cross bear who said the rabbit was cross.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna say Ujjwal was angry on Monday?
qa.a: She was the one feeling cross and grabby, but that felt bad to own, so she said her brother was the angry one.

qa.q: What helped Bhavna name her own feeling by Friday?
qa.a: The bear story let her see, in a fun way, that the cross one can blame someone else, so she could notice it in herself.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel on Friday when Bhavna asks for a turn?
qa.a: Ujjwal probably feels happier and more willing to share when asked kindly.

grounding: Shows a young child placing her own anger onto her brother after snatching his things, and slowly learning to own it.

passage: The train to Chennai was hot and packed, and the family had only one window seat. Kavitha pushed her cousin Divyansh off it and climbed on. Divyansh started to cry. Kavitha pointed at him. "Divyansh is being cross! He's shouting at me!" But Divyansh wasn't shouting. He was sniffling. Her Periamma looked at Kavitha's hot face and tight arms. "Kavitha, I think someone wanted the window very much. Is that you?" Kavitha's lip wobbled. "I'm cross 'cause I want it." "That's okay to feel. You can have it till the big station, then Divyansh."

qa.q: Where was the train going?
qa.a: To Chennai.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha say Divyansh was being cross?
qa.a: She was the one who felt cross and grabby about the window, but owning it felt bad, so she put the angry feeling on him.

qa.q: What did Periamma do that helped in the crowded train?
qa.a: She noticed Kavitha's face and arms, gently named the feeling, and offered a fair plan to share the window.

qa.q: How might Divyansh see what happened?
qa.a: He probably felt pushed and confused, since he was only sniffling, not being cross.

grounding: Shows a young child who pushed a cousin off a seat accusing him of being cross, placing her own anger outside herself.

passage:
It was Holi, and the colony courtyard was full of children with water guns. Omkar, five, snatched a big blue water gun from his friend Arnab.

Arnab started to cry.

Omkar shouted, "You're so mean! You're angry at me!"

Omkar's mother came over. "Omkar, who took the water gun?"

"Arnab is angry! He's being mean!"

She knelt down. "I think you took it, and maybe you feel angry inside."

Omkar's face crumpled. He handed back the gun. "I wanted it."

"I know. Let's ask for a turn."

qa.q: What did Omkar snatch?
qa.a: A big blue water gun.

qa.q: Why did Omkar shout that Arnab was angry and mean?
qa.a: Omkar felt angry and guilty inside, and it felt too bad to own, so he said Arnab was the angry one.

qa.q: What did Omkar's mother do that helped?
qa.a: She calmly named what happened and his feeling, and helped him ask for a turn.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel being called mean after his gun was taken?
qa.a: Arnab probably felt hurt and confused, since he was the one who lost the gun.

grounding: A child who snatched a toy shouts that the other child is mean and angry, placing his own anger outside.

passage:
"Farida! Sudha took my doll!"

"Sudha, did you?"

"No! Farida is angry! She's being mean to me!"

"Sudha, the doll is in your hand."

"Because Farida is angry!"

The Eid lights twinkled on the window. Farida's aunt knelt beside Sudha. "Sudha, I think you wanted the doll very much. And maybe you feel a bit angry and bad inside."

Sudha's lip wobbled. "I wanted it."

"That's okay. Let's ask Farida if you can have a turn."

Sudha held out the doll. "Sorry, Farida."

qa.q: What did Sudha have in her hand?
qa.a: The doll.

qa.q: Why did Sudha say Farida was angry and mean?
qa.a: Sudha felt angry and bad inside about taking the doll, so she put that feeling onto Farida.

qa.q: What did Farida's aunt do that helped Sudha?
qa.a: She gently named Sudha's wanting and angry feeling, then suggested asking for a turn.

qa.q: How might Farida feel when Sudha calls her mean?
qa.a: Farida probably feels upset and confused, since Sudha took her doll.

grounding: A child who took a doll says the other child is angry and mean, placing that unwanted feeling outside.

passage:
Preschool note, Christmas party, by the class teacher.

At the party, Chaitanya grabbed a paper crown from Ayesha's head. When Ayesha cried, Chaitanya shouted, "Ayesha is angry! She's mean!" He kept saying it, even louder.

I knelt beside him. "Chaitanya, I saw you take the crown. I think maybe you feel angry, or bad, inside." He looked at me and his face went red. Then he cried too.

I stayed with him until he calmed down. He gave Ayesha the crown and we made a new one for him. I'll let his parents know today, so they can help at home too.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya grab from Ayesha's head?
qa.a: A paper crown.

qa.q: Why did Chaitanya keep shouting that Ayesha was angry?
qa.a: He felt bad and angry about taking the crown, and it was easier to say those feelings belonged to Ayesha.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Chaitanya?
qa.a: The teacher calmly named what happened and his feelings, stayed with him until he calmed, and helped fix it with a new crown.

qa.q: How might Ayesha feel after getting the crown back?
qa.a: Ayesha probably felt relieved and happy again.

grounding: A teacher notes a child who snatched a crown and then shouted that the other child was angry and mean.

passage: At the village Diwali fair, Imran snatched the little clay elephant out of Kalyani's hands. Kalyani reached for it, and Imran shouted, "You're mean! You're so angry! Go away!" Kalyani blinked; she wasn't shouting at all. Imran's own face was red, his fists tight around the elephant. His Nani came over and knelt between them. "Imran, who has the angry face right now?" Imran looked at his fists. His lip wobbled. "Me," he whispered. Nani nodded. "You wanted the elephant a lot. Let's ask Kalyani for a turn."

qa.q: What did Imran snatch?
qa.a: The little clay elephant.

qa.q: Why did Imran call Kalyani angry?
qa.a: He was the one feeling angry and wanting the elephant, but owning that felt bad, so he put the anger on Kalyani.

qa.q: How did Nani help Imran?
qa.a: She asked who had the angry face, let him notice his own fists, named his wanting, and helped him ask for a turn.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel being called mean?
qa.a: Confused and hurt, since she wasn't shouting and her toy had been taken.

grounding: A preschooler who snatched a toy shouts that the other child is mean and angry.

passage: On a snowy afternoon in a Leipzig park, Esther grabbed the rope of Jana's red sled and pulled. "Mine now!" When Jana held on, Esther yelled, "You're being mean! You're angry at me!" Jana, surprised, let go. Esther's mother crouched down in the snow. "Esther, look at your hands. They're holding very tight. How does your tummy feel?" Esther frowned. "Hot. Grumpy." "That's angry," her mother said gently. "You wanted the sled. Jana isn't angry, she's sad." Esther held the rope a moment longer, then handed it back. "Can I go next?"

qa.q: What colour was Jana's sled?
qa.a: Red.

qa.q: Why did Esther yell that Jana was angry?
qa.a: Esther felt hot and grumpy from wanting the sled, but it felt easier to see the anger in Jana than in herself.

qa.q: How did Esther's mother help?
qa.a: She pointed to Esther's tight hands, asked how her tummy felt, named the anger as Esther's own, and noted that Jana was sad.

qa.q: How does Jana feel when Esther grabs the rope?
qa.a: Surprised and sad, letting go rather than fighting.

grounding: A preschooler who grabbed a sled shouts that the other child is angry, placing her own feeling outside herself.

passage: At the daycare Christmas craft table, Thomas snatched the gold crayon from Lalit. Lalit said, "Hey!" and Thomas shouted, "You're angry! You're a mean boy!" Then he burst into tears, as if he were the one wronged. The teacher knelt beside them. "Thomas, I see a very cross face. Whose face is it?" Thomas touched his own cheeks, wet and hot. "Mine," he said. "You wanted gold for your star," the teacher said. "That's a big want. Lalit, can Thomas use gold after you?" Lalit nodded. Thomas gave the crayon back, sniffing.

qa.q: Which crayon did Thomas snatch?
qa.a: The gold crayon.

qa.q: Why did Thomas burst into tears after calling Lalit mean?
qa.a: He felt angry and a bit guilty about snatching, and seeing the anger in Lalit let him feel like the wronged one.

qa.q: What did the teacher do right?
qa.a: Asked whose face was cross so Thomas could find his own anger, named his want, and arranged a turn.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel being called mean?
qa.a: Confused and upset, since he only said "Hey!" when his crayon was taken.

grounding: A preschooler snatches a crayon and accuses the other child of being angry and mean.

passage:
Before: On the first cold morning of the winter holidays, Anand grabbed Jaya's toy train on the verandah. When she reached for it, he shouted, "You're being mean! You're so angry!" His own fists were tight.
During: Two days later, at their Nani's house, Jaya only looked at the train, and Anand yelled, "Stop being cross at me!"
After: On Sunday, Mummy knelt beside him. "I think Anand feels cross right now." Anand stamped his foot. Then he mumbled, "Me cross," and pushed the train back to Jaya.

qa.q: Where did Anand first grab Jaya's toy train?
qa.a: On the verandah.

qa.q: Why did Anand shout that Jaya was angry?
qa.a: He was angry himself 😠, with tight fists, but owning that feeling was too uncomfortable, so he put it onto Jaya instead.

qa.q: How did Mummy help, and what could she keep doing?
qa.a: She calmly named Anand's feeling without blaming him, which let him say "Me cross"; she can keep putting words to his feelings.

qa.q: What is it like for Jaya to be called mean?
qa.a: It is confusing and unfair, because she only reached for or looked at her own train and gets blamed for anger that is not hers.

grounding: A young child who snatched a toy accuses the other child of being mean and angry, placing his own anger outside himself.
